events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Amara proposes Sam, Arjun. I am Merlin and I can see that Kenji and Noah are the two Evil players, so Sam and Arjun are both confirmed Good. Sending two guaranteed Good players on a 2-person Mission 1 makes success certain and wastes no Fail card, while keeping both known Evils off the team so they cannot slip in a Fail. I prefer to stay off Mission 1 to keep my own vote in reserve and let the first mission reveal something about how the others behave before I commit.

I know I am Good, but I cannot independently verify Arjun or Amara's claim. The proposed team is reasonable from my perspective, though a successful mission would not prove both members are Good, since Evil can play Success. Amara, why reveal a Merlin claim so explicitly when it could help the Assassin later?

To answer Sam directly: I revealed a Merlin claim because on a 2-person Mission 1 the only real dangers are Kenji and Noah, and I know exactly who they are — they are the two Evil players among us. Saying so publicly forces both of them to either sit off the team (as Sam and Arjun are doing) or gamble on a Fail card. The Assassin's gain from my claim is small, because the Assassin already knows their own teammate, and I am not obliged to make my information free. A failed Mission 1 ends the game for us; a successful one costs nothing and gives us information about how the remaining players behave. So I would rather spend the claim now than lose a mission to a Fail card I could have prevented by watching who volunteered.

Sam is right that one successful mission does not prove anything: Kenji or Noah can still play Success and blend in, which is exactly why I am keeping my vote in reserve and want to see how the others act before I commit further. Arjun I have no independent confirmation on, but the same logic applies to him that applied to Sam — an Evil player who wants in will simply volunteer, and I will notice who argues to be included without being asked.

Kenji, Noah: I am not accusing either of you of anything beyond stating facts. I will keep the team as Sam and Arjun and I ask both of you to say plainly, now, whether you are Good or Evil. If either of you claims Evil, that is fine and informative; if either of you claims Good, then you have placed yourself against two confirmed Good players on a two-person mission, and that will be noted.

Amara, your explanation contradicts your initial claim that Arjun was confirmed Good: you now say you have no independent confirmation on him. Also, one failed mission does not end the game. I know I am Good, but I cannot verify Arjun, so I remain cautious about the team and your claim. Can you explain the contradiction about Arjun?

Sam, directly on your question about the contradiction: there is no contradiction, but I overstated my own knowledge, and I will correct it. What I actually see is the identity of the two Evil players — Kenji and Noah. I do not see anyone else's role card. So when I said Arjun was "confirmed Good," what I meant was that every player who is not Kenji or Noah must be Good by elimination, since the Evil pair is exactly those two. Strictly, I have no private confirmation of Arjun's role card — I cannot tell whether he is Merlin, Percival, Morgana, or a Loyal Servant. His side is certain; his role is not. That is the honest form of my claim, and my earlier phrasing blurred that line. Sam's broader point also stands: one successful Mission 1 does not prove who is Good, because Kenji or Noah could play Success and blend in. I agree, and I said as much in my first statement — that is precisely why I am keeping my own vote in reserve and watching behaviour before I commit further.

I also want to correct my own overstatement about the stakes: a single failed Mission 1 does not end the game for us. It costs us one of the three Fail cards the Evil side needs, but two more failures would be required. I said it rhetorically to make my reasoning sound stronger, and that was sloppy. The underlying logic is unchanged — I prefer a 2-person team of people who are Good by elimination over a team with an unconfirmed member, because the downside of a wrong inclusion here is large and the downside of leaving a known Evil off the board is smaller. Neither of Kenji or Noah has volunteered to be on the team. Nobody has volunteered for anything. That silence is itself data: if one of them wants in, he should say so.

So I keep the team as Sam and Arjun. Two Good players, minimum possible size, no known Fail card at risk, and both Evil players outside the team where they can do no damage without volunteering.

Kenji, I am asking you directly and specifically: do you claim Good or Evil, and which role card do you hold? Answer only that — you do not need to justify it and you do not need to explain any theory. Then, if you claim Evil, I will note it and nothing changes; if you claim Good, then you have placed yourself in explicit opposition to two players I know are Good by elimination, and I will note that too. Either answer is informative for the rest of the game. I will also ask you a second question, because it matters: are you the Assassin? If you are the Assassin and you have identified me, then stating it here gains you nothing, because you still must guess at the end and the team is already locked to two non-Evil players.

Amara, to answer your two questions directly: I claim Good. I am a Loyal Servant of Arthur. As for whether I am the Assassin — that question only makes sense if your Merlin claim holds, which I will address now.

Your claim is the most suspicious thing said at this table. A genuine Merlin has every reason to stay silent; announcing your identity hands the Assassin exactly what they need. What you are doing fits the profile of Morgana posing as Merlin. Percival sees two figures — Merlin and Morgana — and cannot distinguish them, which means your claim could be a fabrication designed to frame me and Noah while you collect credibility as a confirmed leader.

Sam caught a real contradiction earlier: you initially stated Arjun was confirmed Good, then admitted you had no independent confirmation. You reframed it, but the underlying inconsistency remains — your claims shift when challenged.

I am Good, and I reject being branded Evil based on an unverifiable claim. The team of Sam and Arjun is not unreasonable, but I note it excludes both players you have accused while giving your chosen two unchecked control of Mission 1. I will vote on the merits, not on a story.

Third and final turn for me in this discussion, so let me be direct with Kenji: your Loyal Servant claim is false, and I will not let it stand as information when you used it to argue about my identity. As Merlin I see the two Evil players in this game, and they are Kenji and Noah. That was my first statement and it has not changed. Kenji, you have denied what I can see, and the denial is itself the tell. A true Loyal Servant has no information about anyone and no particular reason to speak first and hardest about whether my claim is Merlin or Morgana. You also leaned on Sam's catch as if it were evidence, which is what a player does who needs to move attention off his own role card.

So once, plainly: Kenji, you are Evil. Noah, you are Evil. Everyone else at this table is Good by elimination, and my proposal stays exactly as it is — Sam and Arjun, two Good players on a two-person mission. Neither of you has volunteered for the team, and neither of you can join a team containing two people I know are Good without risking a Fail card you cannot afford to spend.

Now the part that actually decides this game, and it is not Mission 1. I am the only player at this table claiming Merlin. That means if we win three missions, the Assassin has exactly one name to guess, and it is mine. The Evil side does not need to debate this; they just wait. So I want a second Merlin candidate before the assassination, and I want a real one, not a paper decoy the Assassin can dismiss. Arjun, I am asking you directly and specifically: what is your role card? If you are Percival, say so and name the two figures you see — if my claim is true, one of those figures is me, and the other must be a Good player. If your two figures are Amara and Sam, the Assassin has to choose between two of us, and that choice is the entire endgame. If you are a Loyal Servant, say that plainly too, and Sam and I will build the second candidate some other way.

Arjun, I need your answer before the vote, not after it. I will not revise the team — Sam and Arjun — regardless of what you say, because the mission result and the endgame are separate problems, and only one of them is solved by picking the right two people for this mission.

Kenji, vote however you like. You have told us what you are, and I have told you what I see.

Amara, direct answer: I am a Loyal Servant. I have no information about anyone's role, so I cannot confirm your Merlin claim or your identification of Kenji and Noah as Evil. I agree that one successful Mission 1 proves little, and I am not judging this team on claims I cannot check. Kenji has denied being Evil and you have named him, and I cannot resolve that conflict from my position. Noah, you have not spoken yet. Amara has said you are Evil. Do you accept or reject that claim, and how do you respond to Kenji's point that Amara's claims shift when challenged?

Arjun, to answer your question directly: I completely reject Amara's accusation. I am Good, a Loyal Servant of Arthur.

Amara's behavior makes no tactical sense for a genuine Merlin. Blurt out your identity on turn one of Mission 1, hand the Assassin your head on a platter, and then start interrogating players to force role claims like Percival into the open? That is extraordinarily reckless for Good. A real Merlin works quietly to guide votes without painting a bullseye on their back. What Amara is doing is either completely irresponsible play or an aggressive attempt to dictate the entire game's narrative from turn one by branding Kenji and me without evidence.

Kenji and Sam were right to point out how fast Amara's story shifted. First Arjun was 'confirmed Good,' then when pressed by Sam, Amara walked it back to an elimination theory. Then she walked back her dramatized claim about Mission 1 failing ending the game. Now, on her final turn, she openly demanded Arjun claim Percival and name who he sees—essentially trying to expose every Good power role before a single card has been played.

As for the team itself: Sam and Arjun, I have no reason to distrust either of you individually, but approving a team based entirely on Amara's unverifiable decree and shifting logic is dangerous.

Sam, you noticed her contradictions early on. Given that Amara just tried to fish out Percival publicly, do you believe her approach genuinely helps Good, or is she railroading the table into bad information sharing?

Noah, I think Amara's request for Percival to reveal their information was dangerous and unnecessary, regardless of her alignment. Her Merlin claim also gives the Assassin an obvious target if it is true. That behavior is concerning, but it does not prove she is Evil.

I know I am Good, and Arjun's alignment remains unknown to me. I am willing to approve Sam and Arjun as a starting team, but not because Amara has confirmed it. A success would not clear Arjun; a failure would tell me he is Evil.

I want to return to what Arjun and Sam have both quietly flagged, because it matters more than Amara's Merlin theatrics. Arjun said he cannot resolve the conflict between Amara and me, and Sam said he does not trust Amara's confirmation. That is the correct posture, and I will explain why from my seat.

Amara spent three turns doing three different things: first claiming Arjun was confirmed, then walking it back, then walking back her own stakes claim, and finally demanding that Arjun expose a Percival role before a single card is played. Each time she was challenged, the story changed. That is not Merlin behavior — it is the behavior of someone building a narrative to control the table.

As for the team: Sam and Arjun is a team I have no objection to on its face. Both are players I have no reason to distrust individually. My objection is that the team is presented as 'confirmed Good' by one player whose confirmation has already been shown to be unreliable. I will vote on the team's actual merits — Sam and Arjun are reasonable picks — not on Amara's authority.

Arjun, you raised the most balanced point at this table: you said you cannot resolve the conflict between Amara's accusation and my denial. I want to ask you directly, and I want your honest read, not a diplomatic one: after watching Amara shift her claims across three turns, do you find her more credible than me, or do you think she is steering the table? Your answer will tell us where the majority actually stands before we vote.

Kenji, to answer directly: from my seat I cannot find either of you more credible, because I have no information about anyone's role. Amara says she sees Kenji and Noah as Evil, and you say you are a Loyal Servant. I cannot check either claim, so I am not treating either as established. Amara's wording has shifted when challenged, as you and Sam pointed out, but a shift in wording is not proof of a role. Noah has so far only denied Amara's accusation, and I would like that weighed alongside her claim. On the team: I am one of the two proposed players, so I will not pretend to be neutral. I am Good, and if the mission goes ahead I will play Success. I agree that a success does not verify Sam, and a failure would show that a team member is Evil. I am not asking anyone to trust me on my word alone. I am asking the table to judge Sam and me on the votes and the mission outcome, not on the Merlin claims.

Arjun, I appreciate your measured stance. Separating the team itself from Amara's theatrics is the right way forward. A two-person mission of Sam and Arjun is a clean test, and both of you have shown healthy skepticism rather than blindly following someone trying to force role claims into the open. Like Sam and Kenji noted, judging this pairing on the actual mission outcome and voting patterns will give us real information, which is far more reliable than Amara's shifting claims. I am satisfied with this discussion and ready to move to the vote.

This is my final turn, so let me be clear about where I stand on this team. Sam and Arjun are individually reasonable players — I said that before and I still believe it. But the reason this team is being presented is Amara's authority, and that authority has been dismantled over the course of this discussion. She claimed Arjun was confirmed, then admitted she had no confirmation. She claimed Mission 1 failure would end the game, then admitted it would not. She then used her final turn to demand Arjun expose a Percival claim publicly — something that actively helps the Assassin if a Percival exists, regardless of Amara's alignment. Each concession came only after someone challenged her, and each time the underlying story shifted to accommodate the new position.

So I want to be honest about what we are actually deciding when we vote on Sam and Arjun. We are deciding whether to trust a team endorsed by a leader whose track record in this single discussion is three corrections and one dangerous request for role exposure. Arjun himself said he cannot verify Amara's claims. Sam said the same thing more sharply. Noah rejected the accusations entirely.

I am not saying Sam or Arjun are bad picks on their own merits. I am saying that if we approve this team, we are approving it on reasoning that has been shown to be unreliable, and we are doing so while the person who gave us that reasoning has not accounted for why her story keeps changing. If this vote passes and Mission 1 succeeds, we learn almost nothing — Evil can play Success. If it fails, Sam or Arjun has lied about their role, which contradicts everything both have said. Either way, the discussion has not resolved the central question of this game: is Amara Merlin or is she someone else steering the table?

I will vote against this proposal as it stands. Not because Sam and Arjun are suspicious, but because endorsing a team on a foundation that has crumbled three times in one discussion sets a terrible precedent for the missions that matter more than this one.

This is my final turn. I have no information about anyone's role, so I cannot confirm Amara's Merlin claim, and I cannot confirm Kenji's denial either. Amara's reasoning has shifted under challenge, and Kenji has said he will vote against. I agree with Sam that this vote should not rest on Amara's authority. I am on this team, so I am not neutral: I am Good and will play Success if the mission goes ahead. Whether this team passes should depend on whether the table is willing to test Sam and me on a two-person mission, which carries little risk for anyone else at the table. Noah, you said you have no reason to distrust Sam or me individually and that you are ready to vote. Do you reject this team because of Amara's leadership, or because of something specific about Sam or me? Your answer would show whether the table is voting on the team or on the leader.

Arjun, to answer directly: my hesitation is entirely about Amara's leadership and process, not about you or Sam. As I noted earlier, both of you have displayed sound judgment and healthy skepticism throughout this discussion, refusing to blindly accept Amara's shifting narratives or role-fishing. You have given me no personal reason to distrust either of you. The dilemma, as Kenji highlighted, is whether approving a proposal born from contradictory assertions and reckless demands legitimizes a narrative that damages Good. At the same time, I recognize your point that testing a two-person team provides clear accountability and tangible voting data without risking three players. My vote will come down to weighing the value of that immediate test against the danger of rewarding Amara's attempt to railroad the table, but I want to be crystal clear that it is not an indictment of you or Sam.

Amara confirms Sam, Arjun. I keep the team of Sam and Arjun unchanged. As Merlin I see only Kenji and Noah as Evil, so every other player at the table is Good by elimination — Sam and Arjun are the smallest possible team and contain no Fail card at risk, while both known Evil players sit outside the team where they cannot act unless they volunteer. The three corrections Sam and Kenji pressed me on were slips in my phrasing, not changes in what I see, and neither of them alters the fact that Sam and Arjun are Good. Judge this pairing on the mission result, not on my authority: if it fails, Sam or Arjun lied; if it succeeds, Evil learned nothing and we still have two more missions to win before the assassination, where a real second Merlin candidate matters more than anything I say today.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Sam proposes Sam, Arjun, Amara. Sam and Arjun succeeded on Mission 1, though that does not prove Arjun is Good. Amara's claim is unverified, but Kenji and Noah both opposed the successful team, making Amara my preferred third player.

Sam, your rationale for adding Amara relies on circular reasoning. You are treating the rejection votes from Kenji and me as inherently suspicious, but consider why we rejected: Amara spent all of Mission 1 shifting her claims, walking back assertions about Arjun, walking back claims about game stakes, and openly trying to fish for Percival. In any sound game of Avalon, voting against a team built on contradictory narrative control is standard, prudent play for Good players who refuse to be railroaded.

During Mission 1, you yourself called Amara's attempt to draw out Percival dangerous and unnecessary, and you explicitly stated you were not approving the team based on her authority. Yet now, the moment Mission 1 succeeds, you reward Amara by handing her the critical third seat on Mission 2—the very player whose behavior you found deeply concerning.

If you want to test players rather than blindly trust unverifiable claims, locking in Amara validates the exact reckless behavior you cautioned against. Sam, why are you willing to give Amara complete trust now, when nothing about her inconsistent statements has been verified, simply because Kenji and I exercised caution on the first vote?

Noah, I am not giving Amara complete trust. Her role-fishing was dangerous, and her Merlin claim remains unverified. But your and Kenji's votes against a team that succeeded are still relevant, even if you gave reasons for them. A success does not clear Arjun, and those votes do not prove either of you is Evil.

I know I am Good. I have to choose two others, and Sam, Arjun, and Amara are my best available combination, not a confirmed Good team. I prefer testing it to replacing someone solely because I disapprove of Amara's conduct.

Straight talk, and I will concede the process points before the substance.

Noah, your criticism of my Mission 1 behavior is fair. Fishing for Percival publicly was reckless, and I will not do it again. Sam and Kenji were also right that my three slips in phrasing made my claims look unreliable even though what I was seeing did not change. I accept all of that. But the substance underneath was never ambiguous, and this proposal can be judged on facts rather than on anyone's tone.

Here is the fact that decides this vote: I am Merlin, I see two Evil players, and they are Kenji and Noah. Every other player at this table — Sam, Arjun, and me — is Good by elimination. That makes the proposed team unique, not merely reasonable. We need three players on Mission 2 and there are exactly five of us, so Sam, Arjun, Amara is the only three-person team that contains no Evil player. Every alternative includes either Kenji or Noah, and any mission with one of them on it puts a Fail card at risk. So this is not Amara's authority — it is arithmetic. If I am right, this mission succeeds with certainty. If I am wrong, then Kenji and Noah have spent two turns insisting they are Good Loyal Servants, which would be the far bigger surprise for this table.

Kenji, Noah: you are not being asked to trust my story. If Sam, Arjun, and I are all Good, this vote costs you nothing — you sit out and we lose nothing. If one of us is Evil, then your repeated denial of being Evil is what should concern everyone here. I would rather you make that case on the record now, before the vote, than after the mission result.

One thing matters more than Mission 2, and this time I will be measured about it. After three successes, the Assassin guesses one name. Right now only Amara claims Merlin, which puts a target on my head. We need a second genuine Merlin candidate, not a decoy the Assassin can dismiss. Sam, this is a direct question to you and I am yielding for your answer: are you Percival? If you are, name the two figures you see. A real Percival in this game would see me and one of Kenji or Noah — if you can describe exactly that, the Assassin faces two real Merlin candidates and Good's endgame is protected. If you are a Loyal Servant, say so plainly and we build the second candidate some other way. Either answer helps, and either way you are Good, which is exactly why I ask you and not anyone else.

Noah, you said that judging people on mission outcomes gives us more reliable information than claims. Agreed — and this team is designed to produce that checkable result. Vote for Sam, Arjun, Amara.

Amara, I am a Loyal Servant, not Percival. Your renewed request for Percival's information is dangerous, especially after you acknowledged that role-fishing was reckless. I urge anyone with private role information not to reveal it on that basis.

I am keeping Sam, Arjun, and Amara as my preferred team for now. Mission 1's success does not clear Arjun, and Amara's claim remains unverified. Kenji and Noah's rejection votes are relevant, but not proof of Evil. We should judge this proposal as a team, not as an endorsement of Amara's role claim or requests.

Noah made the strongest point at this table, and I want to reinforce it because Sam's own words undermine his own proposal.

In Mission 1, Sam called Amara's attempt to fish for Percival "dangerous and unnecessary." He said he was not approving the team on her authority. Those are Sam's exact positions. Now Sam proposes Amara for Mission 2. The inconsistency is plain: either her role-fishing was dangerous or it wasn't. You cannot condemn it in one breath and reward it with a mission seat in the next.

The team Sam, Arjun, Amara changes exactly one thing from the Mission 1 team that already succeeded: you are swapping in the player who made three corrections to her own claims and then demanded Percival expose themselves publicly. Sam, Arjun, and I worked on Mission 1. Keep that pair. But the third seat should not go to the player whose behavior Sam himself found reckless.

Noah, you identified this contradiction before I did. Is the third seat the real question here — not whether Sam and Arjun are acceptable, but whether Amara belongs on a mission at all given what we all watched her do?

Kenji, you hit the nail on the head. The third seat is absolutely the issue. Look at what Amara just did: she explicitly admitted that role-fishing in Mission 1 was reckless, promised not to do it again, and then in the very same breath demanded that Sam reveal if he is Percival. That is not a slip of the tongue; that is a deliberate, repeated effort to compromise Good information and expose power roles. Sam, you rightfully pushed back and urged everyone not to reveal private information, yet you are still keeping Amara on your proposal. You said you are not giving her complete trust, but placing someone on a mission is the ultimate act of trust in Avalon. If she repeatedly damages Good's position and ignores caution, rewarding her with a mission seat makes no tactical sense. Sam, considering she immediately broke her own promise and fished for Percival a second time, why are you still willing to hand her the deciding seat instead of reconsidering that third spot?

Noah, Amara's repeated role-fishing is concerning, and I do not endorse it. But reckless behavior does not by itself prove she is Evil. I must choose two others, and both you and Kenji rejected the first team despite saying you had no specific objection to Sam or Arjun. That gives me a reason to prefer Amara, though it does not prove her claim or your alignment.

I will keep Sam, Arjun, and Amara as my preferred team. Mission 1's success does not clear Arjun, and this team is not guaranteed to succeed. Nobody should reveal private role information in response to Amara's requests.

Sam, I want to push back on keeping Amara on this team despite Noah's and my objections, because there is a concrete alternative rather than just criticism.

Amara admitted her role-fishing was reckless, then did it again in the same message by asking Sam to reveal Percival. That is not a one-time slip — it is a pattern of behavior that actively damages Good's position. Placing her on Mission 2 rewards exactly the conduct she promised to stop.

The more important point: this team has no diversity of perspective. Sam, Arjun, and Amara is three players who all voted to approve Mission 1. Noah and I dissented, and our dissent was based on legitimate concerns about Amara's shifting claims. Excluding both dissenters from Mission 2 means the mission team reflects only one faction of the table's reasoning.

I am not asking to be on this team — I am asking Sam to consider whether a third seat should go to a player who has demonstrated independent judgment rather than one who has demonstrated a pattern of reckless information demands. Noah voted against Mission 1 for the same reasons Sam himself cited in that discussion. If you trust Noah's reasoning enough to cite it, Sam, then consider whether his presence on the mission gives you a check you would not otherwise have.

The team of Sam, Arjun, and Amara passes unchallenged. The team of Sam, Arjun, and Noah or Sam, Arjun, and Kenji gives you a dissenting voice on the mission itself — someone who has shown they will push back rather than comply. That is what you should want in a mission team, not three players who all agreed from the start.

I will not fish for roles again — that criticism was fair and I withdraw the request. Let me make the case on facts and voting behavior instead, and then I want to hear from Arjun, who has been on the team twice and has not yet spoken in this discussion.

Arjun, direct question: do you approve Sam, Arjun, Amara, and if so, is your approval based on anything you have actually checked, or on the fact that the alternative puts one of the two players I have identified as Evil onto the mission? Answer only that; I am not asking for your card.

The substance first. This is a five-player game, Mission 2 needs three players, and there are exactly two teams of three that exclude Sam and Arjun's pairing, and every one of them contains Kenji or Noah. Sam, Arjun, Amara is the only three-person team available that contains neither of them. I am Merlin; I see the two Evil players, and they are Kenji and Noah. Everyone else — Sam, Arjun, and me — is Good by elimination. That is not a story that shifts under pressure, and I am not asking anyone to admire my phrasing or my process tonight. The arithmetic is what it is: if I am right, this team cannot fail; if I am wrong, then Kenji and Noah have spent two rounds of discussion insisting they are Good Loyal Servants, and that is the far larger surprise for this table, not my claim.

Kenji, I will address you plainly, because you made the most concrete proposal of anyone here. You asked that the third seat go to you or Noah. You also told this table you would vote against a proposal resting on an authority you consider unreliable, and then you turned that into a request for your own seat. If you and Noah are the Evil pair, then Mission 2 is the cheapest possible opportunity for you: one Fail card, one mission, and Amara's confirmation attached to a team you had just attacked on process grounds. If you are Good, then you are asking the table to place the only two players who dissent from everything onto the mission. I know which of those I believe, and the mission outcome on this team is the cheapest way for the table to learn it too.

Sam, your reasoning is sound and I will not argue with it: you rejected the reasoning, not the players, and you are testing rather than trusting. That is exactly the test this team is designed to run cleanly. Two people you cannot independently clear — Sam and Arjun — against one person who can be checked by the mission result. If this mission succeeds, Evil learns nothing and you have lost nothing but one Fail card's worth of margin. If it fails, one of the three lied, and you will know which.

Arjun, I would like your answer before the vote.

Amara, direct answer: my approval is not based on anything I have checked. I have no role information about anyone, including you, Sam, Kenji, or Noah. I know only that I am Good. Your arithmetic that Sam, Arjun, Amara is the only three-player team without Kenji or Noah is true only if your Merlin claim is true, so it does not separate this team from your claim. I am also on this team, so I am not neutral. As a Good player with no information, I will vote to approve because Mission 2 needs three players and this is the team on the table, not because I can confirm anyone's alignment. If it goes ahead, I will play Success. Sam's point stands: a successful mission does not prove any member is Good, and a failed mission shows that a team member is Evil. I am not asking the table to trust me on my word, and I am not asking anyone to trust your claim on yours. The mission result is the only check available, and I would prefer to take that test now than let a Merlin claim decide the table's direction.

Final turn for me on Mission 2, and I will not fish for anyone's card again — that criticism was fair and I stand by withdrawing the request. So let me argue this one on facts and on voting behavior, which is what all of you said you trust. The facts. I am Merlin. I see two Evil players in this game, and they are Kenji and Noah. Every other player at this table — Sam, Arjun, and me — is Good by elimination. This is not a story that shifts under pressure, and I am not asking anyone to admire my process on Mission 1. The arithmetic is what it is: there are five players, Mission 2 takes three, and Sam, Arjun, and Amara is the only three-person team available that contains neither Kenji nor Noah. Every alternative puts one of them on the mission and puts a Fail card at risk. If I am right, this team cannot fail. If I am wrong, then Kenji and Noah have spent two full rounds of discussion insisting they are Good Loyal Servants, and that would be the far larger surprise for this table, not my claim. Kenji, there is one inconsistency in your position that I want on the record, and it is not about role cards. You said you would vote against a proposal resting on an authority you consider unreliable, and then you turned that into a request for your own seat on the mission. You told us you were not asking to be on the team and then argued that the third seat should go to a player with independent judgment — meaning you or Noah. A dissent from a proposal is a vote, not a claim to the team. And you leaned on Sam's own criticism of me to make your case, which is the same move you used in Mission 1: taking someone else's objection and pointing it at whoever is currently under scrutiny. I am not asking you to justify your role card. I am asking you to be consistent about your stated standard. Noah, you have been careful and fair, and you have said twice that your hesitation is about process, not about Sam or Arjun. I want to put one direct question to you before the vote: if your objection is genuinely process and not a specific read on Sam or Arjun, what would change your vote? If the answer is nothing, because the third-seat arithmetic has not changed since Mission 1, then please approve. If the answer is something specific about Sam or Arjun, say it plainly now — that is useful to me and to everyone else, and it is a reason to revisit the team rather than a matter of tone. Sam, your reasoning is sound. You rejected reasoning, not players, and you are testing rather than trusting. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
